messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Vignette:
Daniel was thirty-six, married, and working at a retail store when he finally came to treatment, but the story he brought into the room began years earlier with a man-made disaster that had split his life into a before and after. He had been on shift when the event unfolded, close enough to smell smoke and feel the press of bodies moving all at once in a panic he had not anticipated. In his memory, it did not unfold as a smooth sequence so much as a series of sharp, separate images: the first burst of alarm, someone pushing past him at close range, the hard surface of a particular material under his hand as he tried to steady himself, and then another brief picture of people behaving in ways he still found hard to understand. When he talked about it, Daniel rarely described it as a continuous story. He spoke in fragments, as if the event had been captured in still photographs that returned with startling force.

What struck him most, even now, was how real those memories felt. Ordinary moments in his day could seem distant and thin by comparison, while the disaster memory came back with a clarity that made his chest tighten and his face flush with shame. He would say that when he pictured it, it was not like recalling something from the past; it was like being dropped back into the scene with all of its detail intact. The images arrived with a vividness that left him shaken, and with them came a heavy sense of shame that he struggled to put into words. He was embarrassed not only by what had happened around him, but by what he had seen himself doing and how exposed he had felt in the crowd. He had come to believe that the memory said something about him, even though he could not fully explain what that was.

In the months afterward, Daniel tried hard not to think about the trauma. He would catch himself starting to remember and deliberately force his attention elsewhere, snapping his mind shut before the images could take hold. At first he told himself the event had not really happened, or at least not in the way others seemed to describe it, and on better days he insisted it had not been that bad. Those explanations offered him a temporary sense of control, though they never lasted long. The memories still intruded, often without warning, and when they did he could feel himself tensing against them as if bracing for impact. There were moments when the strain became unbearable and he hurt himself physically, not because he wanted to die, but because the sharp bodily pain gave him something else to focus on and briefly interrupted the relentless return of the event.

His daily life narrowed over time. As a retail worker, he could not always avoid the press of customers or the closeness of the stockroom and checkout lanes, and that physical proximity now carried a particular charge for him. He became aware of how fast people moved around him, how near strangers stood in line, how easily a shoulder could brush past his arm. At work he found himself scanning the aisle for any sign of crowding or pushing, wary of being trapped again in the kind of space where he had once felt helpless. He also noticed a strange, specific reaction to a texture that reminded him of the event. If his hand met it unexpectedly in the store, something in him recoiled before he could stop it, and the sensation could pull him straight back into that day. He did not tell many people this, but he began altering small routines to reduce the chance of encountering it, which sometimes made his work slower and more difficult.

Another thing that unsettled him was how strongly he reacted to people misbehaving. If he saw customers cutting lines, shouting, shoving, or acting selfishly, the anger and revulsion came fast and hot. It was not just annoyance; it felt to him like a flash of the same moral ugliness he had witnessed during the disaster, when panic had stripped people down to their worst impulses. Those moments could leave him withdrawn and tense for hours. At home, his wife noticed that he was more distant and that he would sometimes stop mid-conversation, as if he had been pulled back into something far away. Daniel was not sure how to explain that he was still living with the event in these small, intrusive ways, especially because part of him still kept insisting it had not truly been as bad as his memory made it seem.

By the time he sought help, the strain had become too hard to hide. The shame, the vivid fragments, the effort of pushing the memories away, and the moments of physical self-harm used to cut off the thoughts had all begun to feel unmanageable. What brought him in was a growing fear that he could not keep handling it alone, and that one day the memories would overtake him in front of his wife or at work. More than anything, he hoped for some way to stop feeling as if he were being dragged back into that disaster every time he was too close to someone, saw people behaving badly, or touched something that brought it all rushing back.
